newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - Jan 21.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - Jan 21.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

The Australian Industrial Relations Commission certified a 10 per cent base pay rise this year for employees of the heavy engineering firm Goninan and Co Ltd. The enterprise deal negotiated with metal industry unions for workers at the Hexham plant near Nwcastle secures further increases of up to two per cent in 1998 based on "productivity milestones". Page 2. --

A State Government scheme to wipe out Aboriginal native land title in common law will be presented to Prime Minister John Howard in a special conference in Sydney tomorrow. Under the plan Aboriginal native title rights would be inscribed in legislation, allowing limited access to pastoral leases in Western Australia, Queensland and the Northern Territory. Page 3.

Australian companies may have to lodge conditional bids for airports because of a problem with the Foreign Takeovers Act. Some major Australian companies, such as Brambles Industries and Lend Lease, are categorised as foreign owned under the Foreign Takeovers Act because of increasing foreign portfolio investments on their registers. Companies categorised as foreign owned must seek Foreign Investment Review Board approval for their acquisitions. The Federal Finance Minister John Fahey may not be able to sove the problem before the January 30 deadline for first round tenders in the A$3 billion airport sale. Page 3.

A university study has shown low income households are hardest hit by last year's Federal budget measures. The Melbourne University study found high income households suffered the most absolute losses, low income households suffered the most relative losss, while middle income households were the least affected. The study was commissioned by the Australian Council of Social Service and the Australian Council of Trade Unions. Page 4.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Prime Minister John Howard yesterday called a special meeting of State and Territory leaders to discuss a "common-sense" response to the High Court's Wik native title ruling. Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory are expected to presen a common position that would see Aborigines' common law entitlements swapped for statutory access rights and the Prime Minister is believed to be open to all proposals for change to native title rights. Page 1.

Speaking yesterday at the launch of Sydney University's Research Institute for Humanities and Social Sciences, the University's vice-chancellor, Professor Gavin Brown, rejected the argument that universities were merely paths to high income for graduates nd catalysts for economic growth. Historian Professor Donald Horne also thought universities should concentrate on the idea of "knowledge" - a word he said had been left out of Education Minister Amanda Vanstone's debate for education funding. Page 1.

Speaking on the John Laws radio program yesterday, Federal Health Minister Michael Wooldridge agreed it was "irresponsible" of parents to not immunise their children and said one in 4000 children who were not vaccinated against whooping cough were likely to die. Wooldridge called on all Health Ministers to be more aggressive in promoting the importance of immunisation. Page 3.

The Australian Wheat Board announced yesterday that the 1996 wheat crop was expected to come in at a record 23 million tonnes, with returns expected to lift by A$3 a tonne for most grades of wheat. The AWB is also forecasting wheat exports of close to 17million tonnes, an improvement on the 13 million tonnes recorded in recent years. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Having called a Premiers meeting in Sydney tomorrow to debate the Wik judgement, Prime Minister John Howard faces a demand from the conservative States for Federal legislation to cancel native title rights on pastoral leases. Some of Howard's Federal coleagues will also push for further amendments to the Native Title Act and the Racial Discrimination Act to give farmers and miners certainty over land management. Page 1.

Arriving at a South African courthouse yesterday to face an extradition hearing, Philip Bell vowed to return to Australia to fight child sex charges, claiming he was not a pedophile. Bell has been on the run from the New South Wales Police Royal Commissin since April last year. Page 1.

Macquarie Bank senior executive Simon Hannes was arrested last week and charged with avoiding laws governing large cash transactions, following a three-month investigation into unusual trading in TNT stock in the lead-up to last year's A$2 billion takeover bid for the transport giant. Page 1.

Rejecting community calls for the A$600 million Eastern Tollway extension to be placed underground from Drivers Triangle, the New South Wales Government is instead considering a proposal that replaces the original eight to 10-lane ground level plan with a two-level roadway, including four lanes of motorway six metres below street level along South Dowling Street. Page 3.
THE AGE

The Australasian Council of Auditor-Generals has condemned the Victorian Government's review of that State's auditor-general. The Victorian Government is reviewing the Audit Act because it is considered to be anti-competitive under national competition gudelines. The review will look at allowing Government departments to appoint their own accountants. The Council says this could jeopardise departmental accountability and the independence of the auditor. Page A1.

Firefighters battled more than 50 fires around Victoria yesterday as temperatures reached 41.2 degrees Celsius. Two houses were destroyed at Mt Eliza and two carports, a car and a barn were burnt at Langwarrin. The worst fires were at Mt Martha on the Morignton Peninsula as 350 firefighters with 65 trucks and four helicopters fought the blaze. Residents near Mt Martha, including 70 scouts, had to be evacuated before the fire was brought under control. Page A1.

Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett has called for tax reforms, including a consumption tax, to be on the agenda for the next Federal election. Speaking on ABC radio yesterday, Kennett acknowledged Prime Minister John Howard's promise not to introduce new taxs in his present term in office. Kennett advocated a consumption tax of well below 15 per cent and called for a commitment on a tax reform agenda. Page A1.

Blanket extinguishment of native title on pastoral leases will not be considered by the Federal Government because of legal and political complexities. The Government will not formally rule out any options on native title, but The Age has reported that Feeral Cabinet has known since April that extinguishment was not viable. Page A3.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
